items.title: EDTA can pull rust out of a bridge
items.claim: EDTA is a hexadentate ligand — it wraps around metal ions with six binding sites and stabilises them dramatically against precipitation. Add EDTA to a rusty surface and it pulls iron(III) into solution as a soluble complex.
items.prompt: Why is a chelating ligand so much more effective than six water molecules?

options.text: EDTA forms covalent bonds; water just hydrogen-bonds
Replacing six independent water ligands with one hexadentate EDTA releases six water molecules into bulk solvent — entropy increases dramatically, driving the equilibrium toward the chelate

items.reveal:
Suppose [Fe(H2O)6]3+ + EDTA4- in solution. The product is [Fe(EDTA)]- plus six free water molecules. Even though Fe-O bonds in the EDTA complex are not radically stronger than Fe-O bonds with water, the entropy change is large and positive — one big complex plus six free waters is much more disordered than seven loose particles.

Formation constants for EDTA complexes typically exceed 10 to the 20 — extraordinarily stable.

Applications: EDTA in cleaning products removes iron and calcium stains; in food (E385) it prevents metal-catalysed oxidation; in medicine, it treats lead and mercury poisoning by chelating the toxic metal so the kidneys can excrete it.
items.why: Bond strength is the obvious explanation. Entropy of releasing many small ligands at once is what really stabilises chelates.

items.title: Hot and cold packs and pottery glazes — all transition metal d-orbital splitting
items.claim: Aqueous Cu(II) is blue. Co(II) is pink in water, blue in concentrated HCl. Cr(III) is violet in water, green in chloride. Same metal ions, different colours depending on what surrounds them.
items.prompt: Why do transition metal complexes have colour at all?

options.text: They reflect light from their metal surface

In a ligand field the five d-orbitals split into sets separated by an energy gap; visible photons matching that gap can excite d-d transitions, and the colour you see is the complement of the absorbed wavelength
Transition metals always emit coloured light spontaneously

items.reveal:
In an octahedral field of six ligands, the d-orbitals split into two sets: lower-energy t2g (dxy, dxz, dyz) and higher-energy eg (dz2, dx2-y2). The energy gap is called Δ (or 10 Dq).

The size of Δ depends on the ligand — the spectrochemical series ranks them: I- < Br- < Cl- < F- < OH- < H2O < NH3 < CN-. Strong-field ligands give larger Δ and absorb shorter wavelengths.

For [Cu(H2O)6]2+, Δ absorbs orange light (~620 nm), transmitting blue. For [CuCl4]2-, the smaller Δ absorbs red, transmitting yellow-green. Same Cu2+, different complement.

Cobalt chloride 'invisible ink' (pink when wet, blue when dry) flips between [Co(H2O)6]2+ (octahedral, weaker field) and [CoCl4]2- (tetrahedral, fewer ligands).
items.why: Transition metal colour is treated as a property of the element. It's actually a property of the coordination environment.

items.title: A copper ion is colourless — and blue, and green
items.claim: Anhydrous CuSO4 is white. Add water and it turns vivid blue. Dissolve in concentrated HCl and it goes yellow-green. Same copper ion, drastically different colours.
items.prompt: What changes when ligands swap around the same Cu2+ centre?

options.text: Different ligands split the d-orbitals by different energies, so the wavelengths of light absorbed change, and the colour observed is the complementary colour of that wavelength
Water and chloride dissolve the copper, removing the colour

items.reveal_title: Crystal field theory — the geometry of d-orbitals
items.reveal:
Cu2+ has 9 d-electrons. In an octahedral field of ligands, the five d-orbitals split into two sets separated by an energy gap (delta-octahedral). A d-electron absorbs a photon and is promoted across this gap.

The gap depends on the ligand — the spectrochemical series ranks them: I- less than Br- less than Cl- less than H2O less than NH3 less than CN-. Larger gaps absorb shorter wavelengths. Cu(H2O)6 2+ absorbs orange (delta corresponding to ~600 nm), so it transmits blue. CuCl4 2- has a smaller gap, absorbs red, transmits yellow-green.

Anhydrous Cu2+ in CuSO4 has no significant ligand field at all — no splitting big enough for visible absorption — and so the salt is white.
items.why: Colour is treated as a fixed property of an element. It's actually a property of the coordination environment around a single ion.
